intro.heading_en: The Praise by Indra and the Gods (Śakrādi Stuti)
intro.carita: Madhyama Carita (the middle episode, chapters 2–4), of which this is the closing chapter. In the recitation tradition the middle carita’s presiding form is Mahālakṣmī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 2), not a statement of the Purāṇa text, which does not use the name Mahālakṣmī here. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 4 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna: one should meditate on Durgā called Jayā, dark as a black cloud, whose sidelong glances bring fear to the hosts of enemies, the crescent moon bound on her crown, holding in her hands conch, discus, sword and trident, three-eyed, seated on the lion’s shoulders, filling the three worlds with her radiance, surrounded by the gods and served by those who seek siddhis.
intro.summary: Medhas resumes (4.1). With Mahiṣa and his army slain, Indra and the gods, bowed and thrilling with joy, praise the Devī (4.2). Their hymn (4.3–23) bows to Ambikā, whose form is the gathered powers of all the gods but who pervades the world by her own power (4.3), whose majesty not even Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva can tell (4.4); she is fortune in the homes of the good and misfortune in the homes of the wicked, understanding, faith and modesty (4.5). The gods cannot describe her form, valour or deeds (4.6), yet name her: the cause of the worlds and the primal Prakṛti (4.7), Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8), the knowledge that liberates (4.9), the Veda whose self is sound, and Vārttā, livelihood (4.10), Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī (4.11). They recall the battle: that Mahiṣa could look on her gentle, moon-like face and still strike, and that he did not die at the sight of it in anger (4.12–13), and they pray for her grace, having seen what her anger does (4.14). Her favour brings honour, wealth and a household at peace (4.15), heaven to the doer of good (4.16), and freedom from fear to whoever remembers her (4.17). Why she kills with weapons and not with a glance: so that even her enemies, purified, reach heaven (4.18–19); their eyes were spared because they gazed at her face (4.20); compassion and relentlessness are found together in her alone (4.21–22); the worlds are saved, the enemies sent to heaven, the gods’ fear gone (4.23). In four anuṣṭubh verses they ask her protection with trident, sword, bell and bow, in every quarter, through her gentle and terrible forms and all her weapons (4.24–27). Medhas tells how the gods worshipped her with flowers of Nandana, perfumes and incense (4.28–30). The Devī offers a boon (4.31–32); the gods answer that nothing remains to be done now that Mahiṣa is dead, but ask that, whenever remembered, she destroy their calamities, and that she increase the wealth and household of any mortal who praises her with these hymns (4.33–37). Saying ‘So be it’, Bhadrakālī vanishes (4.38–39). Medhas closes the story of her rising from the gods’ bodies and announces the next: how she arose again from Gaurī’s body to slay Śumbha and Niśumbha (4.40–42).
intro.forms: Ambikā, ‘the Mother’, the name the gods use most (4.3, 4.24, 4.27, 4.37); Caṇḍikā (4.4, 4.25); Bhagavatī (4.9, 4.10, 4.34) and the sovereign titles Īśvarī (4.25) and Maheśvarī (4.35). In the hymn she is named as qualities and powers: Śrī and Alakṣmī, Buddhi, Śraddhā and Lajjā (4.5); the primal, unmanifest Prakṛti with the three guṇas (4.7); Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8); the supreme Vidyā, cause of liberation (4.9); Trayī, the Veda, whose self is sound (शब्दात्मिका), and Vārttā (4.10); Medhā, Durgā, Śrī as Viṣṇu’s consort and Gaurī as Śiva’s (4.11). The gods address her as Durgā (4.17) and as giver of boons (वरदे, 4.22), liken her angry face to Death (Antaka) enraged (4.13), and ask the protection of her gentle and her terrible forms alike (4.26). In the narrative she is ‘the sustainer of the worlds’ (जगतां धात्री, 4.29), gracious of face (प्रसादसुमुखी, 4.30), and, as she vanishes, Bhadrakālī (4.39).
intro.significance: The chapter turns the victory of chapter 3 into praise, and the praise into a promise. Its hymn is the first in the text addressed to the Goddess as warrior — Brahmā’s hymn in chapter 1 was to Yoganidrā within the sleeping Viṣṇu — and it says what the battle meant: the gods did not lend her their power (4.3), and her killing is itself compassion (4.18–23). The boon the gods ask (4.36–37) is the first statement in the text of the fruit of reciting it, which the Goddess sets out at length in chapter 12. The closing verses (4.40–42) end the middle carita and announce the third, so that the chapter is both an ending and a hinge.
intro.grammar: Most of the hymn (4.2–23) is in vasantatilakā, fourteen syllables to a printed line, so words and junctions often run across a line-end (दोषै- / र्न, 4.7; एत- / न्नीतं, 4.14; भवतीप्रसादा- / ल्लोकत्रये, 4.16); the petitions (4.24–27) return to anuṣṭubh. The hymn style is relative and correlative (या … तां त्वाम्, 4.5; यस्याः … सा, 4.4; यानि … तैः, 4.26–27), with predicates in the nominative and असि understood or stated (मेधासि, दुर्गासि, 4.11). The Goddess is the subject of second-person passives (ज्ञायसे, 4.7; उच्चार्यसे, 4.8; अभ्यस्यसे, 4.9); impersonal passives carry the wonders of the battle (प्रहृतम्, 4.12; कैर्जीव्यते, 4.13). Prayer uses the imperative (प्रसीद, पाहि, रक्ष), deliberation the first-person imperative (किं वर्णयाम, 4.6), courtesy the passive imperative (व्रियताम्, 4.32) and the respectful third person (भवती, भगवत्या). The gods’ boons are asked in epic ātmanepada optatives (हिंसेथाः, भवेथाः, 4.36–37), with the repeated participle संस्मृता संस्मृता ‘each time remembered’ (4.36).
intro.teaching: Literally, the gods praise the Goddess who has saved them, worship her, ask two boons, and she grants them and disappears; Medhas then announces the next story. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the hymn as a statement of who the Goddess is: one power behind fortune and misfortune, intellect and faith, sacrifice and liberation (4.5–4.11), whose anger and grace are one act — she destroys the asuras and purifies them in the same stroke (4.18–4.23). It also draws from the boon that remembrance and the recitation of these verses are enough to draw her help (4.17, 4.36–4.37). A modern reflection, which is ours and not the text’s, might add that the gods, once rescued, ask first for nothing and then for others: every mortal who will say their words. The text itself states only the hymn, the worship, the boons and her promise.
themes: The Goddess is not the sum of the gods’ powers
One Devī in fortune, intellect, faith and the Veda

conclusion.narrative: With Mahiṣa dead, the gods do what they could not do in battle: they praise. Their hymn moves from what she is — beyond the triad’s telling, Prakṛti, Svāhā and Svadhā, liberating knowledge, Veda and livelihood, Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī — to what she did, and finds in the killing a mercy that sent even her enemies to heaven. They ask her protection on every side, worship her, and, offered a boon, ask that she come whenever remembered and bless whoever recites these hymns. ‘So be it,’ says Bhadrakālī, and vanishes. Medhas closes the middle story and announces the last: her rising from Gaurī to slay Śumbha and Niśumbha (4.41–42).

vocabulary.en: a hymn of praise (स्तवैरेभिः, ‘with these hymns’, 4.36)
power; the Goddess’s own power (आत्मशक्तिः) and the gods’ powers gathered in her form (4.3)
primal nature, the unmanifest source of the world (4.7)
one of the three strands of Prakṛti (त्रिगुणा, 4.7)
the call with which offerings go to the gods (4.8)
the call with which offerings go to the ancestors (4.8)
knowledge, here the knowledge that is the cause of liberation (4.9)
intelligence that grasps the śāstras; the Goddess named as it (4.11)
‘hard to reach’: the Goddess as the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean (4.11, 4.17)
gentle, moon-like; set against घोर, terrible (4.26)

constructions: The relative–correlative hymn: a या / यस्याः / यया clause taken up by तां त्वाम्, सा or ताम् (4.3–4.5), and यानि … तैः (4.26–4.27).
Second-person passives with the Goddess as subject and the agent in the instrumental (हरिहरादिभिः … न ज्ञायसे, 4.7; जनैः उच्चार्यसे, 4.8; मुनिभिः अभ्यस्यसे, 4.9).
The impersonal passive: प्रहृतं … महिषासुरेण (4.12), कैर्जीव्यते (4.13), विज्ञातम् (4.14).
Imperatives of prayer (प्रसीद, परिपालय, पाहि, रक्ष) and of deliberation (किं वर्णयाम, 4.6; केनोपमा भवतु, 4.22); the passive imperative of courtesy (व्रियताम्, 4.32).
The concessive imperative with नाम, and a thought closed by इति with मत्वा (कुर्वन्तु नाम … मत्वेति, 4.18).
The participle as a condition (स्मृता, 4.17) and its repetition for ‘every time’ (संस्मृता संस्मृता, 4.36).
Epic ātmanepada forms where classical prose has parasmaipada: हिंसेथाः, भवेथाः (4.36–37), शृणुष्व (4.42).
Agent nouns in -in and -tṛ, the latter with a genitive object (असुरक्षयकारि, 4.6; परमार्तिहन्त्री, 4.10; हन्तृ हृतदेवपराक्रमाणाम्, 4.21; धात्री, 4.29).
insights: Her form was made of the gods’ gathered powers, yet she pervades the world by her own (आत्मशक्त्या, 4.3), and even Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva cannot tell her majesty (4.4, 4.7).
One Goddess is fortune and misfortune, understanding, faith and modesty (4.5), and Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī are she alone (4.11).
The ritual word, liberating knowledge and ordinary livelihood are all her forms: Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8), the supreme vidyā (4.9), the Veda and Vārttā (4.10).
Her severity is her compassion: she slays with weapons so that the slain are purified and reach heaven (4.18–4.19, 4.23), and mercy and relentlessness are seen together in her alone (4.21–4.22).
The gentle and the terrible are one face: the moon-like face Mahiṣa struck and the angry one he survived (4.12–4.13); both kinds of form are asked to protect (4.26).
Remembrance suffices: remembered, she removes the fear of every creature (4.17), and the boon makes remembrance and recitation the way to her help (4.36–4.37).
conclusion.srividya: The hymn shares many names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Ambikā (4.3; name 295, अम्बिका), Svāhā and Svadhā side by side (4.8; names 535, स्वाहा, and 536, स्वधा), Medhā, Durgā and Gaurī (4.11; names 538, मेधा, 190, दुर्गा, and 635, गौरी), Lajjā (4.5; name 740, लज्जा), the Prakṛti of the three guṇas (4.7; names 397, मूलप्रकृतिः, and 984, त्रिगुणा), Trayī (4.10; name 872, त्रयी), Caṇḍikā (4.4, 4.25; name 755, चण्डिका) and Maheśvarī (4.35; name 750, महेश्वरी). The Lalitā Sahasranāma’s अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः (name 992) is close in idea to the compassion of 4.21. These are a shared Śākta vocabulary, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The Śrī of 4.11 is Viṣṇu’s consort, not the Śrī of Śrīvidyā, and no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine — mantra, yantra or the worship of Lalitā — is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: The gods bow to Ambikā, whose form is the gathered powers of all the gods but who pervades the world by her own power.
She is Śrī in the homes of the virtuous and Alakṣmī in those of the wicked, understanding, faith and modesty.
Cause of the worlds, untouched by the faults of the guṇas, the whole world a portion of her: the primal, unmanifest Prakṛti.
Medhā, Durgā the boat across the ocean of existence, Śrī in Viṣṇu’s heart, Gaurī with Śiva — ‘you alone’.
Remembered, Durgā removes the fear of every creature and gives the untroubled a good mind: who but she is so tender to all?
Her nature is to end the ways of the wicked; in slaying them she has shown compassion even to her enemies.
The boon: remembered again and again, may she destroy our calamities — and the promise for whoever praises her with these hymns, completed in 4.37.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi throughout: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (सद्यो विनाशयसि, 4.14; पाहि नो देवि, 4.24), -ḥ → r after other vowels (दोषैर्न, 4.7; नौरसङ्गा, 4.11; कैर्जीव्यते, 4.13), -ḥ → s/ś before t/c (प्रकृतिस्त्वम्, 4.7; हरश्च, 4.4), and -āḥ losing its visarga before voiced sounds and vowels (सुरगणा निहते, 4.2; देवा ऊचुः, 4.33).

Visarga kept before a sibilant where assimilation is optional (नताः स्म, 4.3; श्रीः स्वयम्, 4.5; स्वस्थैः स्मृता, 4.17; निहतः शत्रुः, 4.35), and निश्शेष with the assimilated sibilant (4.3, the variant reads निःशेष).
Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (निहतेऽतिवीर्ये, 4.2; रिपवोऽपि, 4.19; तेऽम्बिके, 4.27), and the double avagraha for ā + ā (सदाऽऽर्द्रचित्ता, 4.17; तथाऽऽत्मनः, 4.39; मयाऽऽख्यातम्, 4.42).
Junctions across the printed line-end of the vasantatilakā stanzas (दोषै- / र्न, 4.7; तृप्तिहेतु- / रुच्चार्यसे, 4.8; एत- / न्नीतम्, 4.14; कर्मा- / ण्यत्यादृतः and भवतीप्रसादा- / ल्लोकत्रये, 4.16).

Consonant sandhi: t + ś → cch and ch doubled (उद्यच्छशाङ्कसदृशच्छवि, 4.13; तच्छृणुष्व, 4.42), t → n before n (यन्न, 4.13; यन्नागता, 4.20), t + l → ll (4.16), n + t → ṃst (अस्मांस्तथा, 4.26), and r before r dropped (तै रक्ष, 4.26).
One declared hiatus: आत्मशूलस्य | उत्तरस्याम् at the pāda break of 4.25, a metrical licence.
samasa: Long bahuvrīhis describing the gods and the Goddess (प्रणतिनम्रशिरोधरांसाः, प्रहर्षपुलकोद्गमचारुदेहाः, 4.2; निश्शेषदेवगणशक्तिसमूहमूर्त्या, 4.3; कैटभारिहृदयैककृताधिवासा, शशिमौलिकृतप्रतिष्ठा, 4.11).
Nañ compounds of the ineffable (अतुलम्, 4.4; अचिन्त्यम्, 4.6; अपारा, अव्याकृता, 4.7; अविचिन्त्यम्, अतुल्यम्, 4.21).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with agent nouns in -in (असुरक्षयकारि, 4.6; दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि, 4.17; शत्रुभयकारि, 4.22; जगत्त्रयहितैषिणी, 4.40).
Nested ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas of light (खड्गप्रभानिकरविस्फुरणैः, शूलाग्रकान्तिनिवहेन, 4.20) and of distress (परमार्तिहन्त्री, 4.10).
Bahuvrīhis in आदि (शक्रादयः, 4.2; हरिहरादिभिः, 4.7; खड्गशूलगदादीनि, 4.27; धनदारादि-, 4.37) and itaretara dvandvas (ऋग्यजुस्, 4.10; आत्मजभृत्यदाराः, 4.15; शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, 4.41).
One avyayībhāva (प्रतिदिनम्, 4.16) and karmadhārayas of title (महेश्वरि, 4.35; भद्रकाली, 4.39).
grammar_notes: नताः स्म (4.3, 4.5) is read as ‘we are bowed’, स्म for स्मः without its visarga, as the metre requires a light syllable.
Epic ātmanepada forms are kept as ārṣa: the optatives हिंसेथाः and भवेथाः (4.36–37) and the imperative शृणुष्व (4.42).
Sentences run across verses: 4.29–4.30 (one subject, verb प्राह), 4.35–4.37 (condition, boon and the reciter’s blessing), 4.41–4.42 (the announcement of the third story).
In 4.25 the south is named with the masculine/neuter locative दक्षिणे beside the feminine locatives of the other quarters, and उत्तर is declined like a pronoun (उत्तरस्याम्).
विलोकयताम् (4.20) is a present participle in the genitive plural agreeing with असुराणाम्, not an imperative; ते in 4.23 is two words, ‘they’ and ‘to you’.
दृष्टा (4.22) agrees with the nearer of two subjects; अस्मत्तः (4.32) is the Goddess’s plural of herself.
themes: The Goddess beyond the gods’ powers
Her forms in fortune, mind and Veda
Gentle and terrible in one face
Remembrance and the fruit of recitation
uncertain: 4.3: निश्शेष (Gita Press, kept) / निःशेष (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the same word.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading, are flagged on 4.3 (नताः स्म as ‘we are bowed’ or the particle स्म), 4.6 (the locative सर्वेषु … असुरदेवगणादिकेषु), 4.7 (दोषैः as ‘by faults’ or as agent) and 4.37 (the construction of वित्तर्द्धिविभवैः).
